title: What can you say about acacia fiber in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 2 wordings for acacia fiber; the strongest is "A prebiotic fibre that helps feed beneficial gut bacteria such as bifidobacteria" (moderate, 10-20 g a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Relieves IBS".

supported_wordings.wording: A prebiotic fibre that helps feed beneficial gut bacteria such as bifidobacteria.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it at 10-20 g a day, citing human studies; no other listed source covers it.

supported_wordings.wording: A source of fibre that supports a healthy digestive system and digestive regularity.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older, as part of a fibre-containing diet for the regularity wording. Health Canada: at least 4 g of fibre a day may be called a high source and 6 g a very high source.

wordings_to_avoid.why: Health Canada lists no constipation dose for acacia, and FDA's 2000 rule clears only the 'occasional' form.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
